Previous prerequisiteChoosing and Checking Cell-Type Annotation Methods▤BrowseAll tutorialsSeveral directionsChoose a next step

Cell annotation tools assign labels by comparing a query dataset with learned classes, reference profiles, or embedded representations. Treat each assignment as a proposal: its usefulness depends on what the model or reference contains and whether the evidence fits your cells.

Format: Advanced template. For readers familiar with Python and AnnData who already have an authorized, human immune-cell .h5ad query with documented raw counts and gene symbols. You will run one CellTypist prediction, save reviewable labels and diagnostics, and inspect reference fit; the input is prepared by you, not supplied here.

Choose a method by its input and comparison

These methods do not share one interchangeable “AI annotation” interface. CellTypist is a logistic-regression classifier with downloadable or custom models. SingleR transfers labels by comparing query expression with a labeled reference. The published CELLama method converts ranked expressed genes, and optionally metadata, into text for sentence-transformer embeddings; the study evaluates embedding-based cell typing against reference cells. Geneformer and scGPT are separate projects with distinct representations and task workflows. A model's general-purpose or foundation-model label does not establish support for every annotation task.

This advanced template expects a reader-prepared my_data.h5ad: AnnData with cells in rows, genes in columns, and an explicitly documented raw-count matrix. mkdir -p celltypist-review
cd celltypist-review

Primary R route: annotate against a labeled reference with SingleR

This is a reproducible R reference-transfer baseline, not an R implementation of CellTypist and not a foundation-model prediction. Prepare two SingleCellExperiment objects from public or synthetic inputs only: query_sce.rds and reference_sce.rds. Both must contain a logcounts assay with compatible gene identifiers; the reference must have a reviewed cell_type label in colData. This template uses those existing log-normalized assays as supplied. It does not normalize, map gene identifiers, choose labels, or fetch data. Review reference provenance, species, tissue, assay, and label granularity before running.

# Inputs: query_sce.rds and reference_sce.rds, prepared by the reader
# Output: singleR_predictions.csv and singleR_scores.csv
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(SingleCellExperiment)
  library(SingleR)
})

query <- readRDS("query_sce.rds")
reference <- readRDS("reference_sce.rds")
if (!inherits(query, "SingleCellExperiment") || !inherits(reference, "SingleCellExperiment")) {
  stop("Both RDS inputs must contain SingleCellExperiment objects")
}
if (!"logcounts" %in% assayNames(query) || !"logcounts" %in% assayNames(reference)) {
  stop("Both objects must contain the declared logcounts assay")
}
if (!"cell_type" %in% colnames(colData(reference))) {
  stop("Reference needs a reviewed cell_type label column in colData")
}
labels <- as.character(colData(reference)$cell_type)
if (anyNA(labels) || any(!nzchar(labels))) {
  stop("Reference labels must be present and non-empty")
}
shared_genes <- intersect(rownames(query), rownames(reference))
if (length(shared_genes) < 2L) {
  stop("Too few exact shared gene identifiers; resolve the feature contract first")
}
query <- query[shared_genes, ]
reference <- reference[shared_genes, ]
if (anyDuplicated(rownames(query)) || anyDuplicated(rownames(reference))) {
  stop("Resolve duplicate gene identifiers before annotation")
}
if (is.null(colnames(query)) || anyDuplicated(colnames(query))) {
  stop("Query cell names must be present and unique")
}
if (is.null(colnames(reference)) || anyDuplicated(colnames(reference))) {
  stop("Reference cell names must be present and unique")
}
prediction <- SingleR(test = query, ref = reference, labels = labels,
                     assay.type.test = "logcounts", assay.type.ref = "logcounts",
                     prune = TRUE)
results <- data.frame(
  cell_id = rownames(prediction),
  label = prediction$labels,
  pruned_label = prediction$pruned.labels,
  delta_next = prediction$delta.next,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
write.csv(results, "singleR_predictions.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(as.data.frame(prediction$scores), "singleR_scores.csv", row.names = TRUE)
message("Annotated ", nrow(results), " query cells using ", length(shared_genes),
        " exact shared genes. Review labels, score separation, pruning, and reference fit.")

Run only after confirming the input contracts and package versions for your environment. A pruned/unassigned label is a useful uncertainty signal, not a failure to be filled automatically. Inspect score patterns, marker evidence, and reference fit; a technically successful transfer is not independent validation and cannot recover cell states absent from the reference.

Optional Python-only method: run and inspect CellTypist

CellTypist inference in this section is Python-only; it is a distinct classifier route, not a matching implementation of the R SingleR baseline. Do not interpret the two tools' scores as interchangeable. CellTypist’s input and model compatibility requirements below apply only to this optional method.

This optional Python template expects a reader-prepared my_data.h5ad made from public or synthetic data only: AnnData with cells in rows, genes in columns, and an explicitly documented raw-count matrix. Start in a dedicated working directory, create an isolated Python environment, and install the two packages (current releases and dependency resolution may change):

mkdir -p celltypist-review
cd celltypist-review
python3 -m venv .venv

tutorials/advanced-ai-single-cell.html.before:
• Reference mismatch: a human immune model is not suitable simply because the query contains immune cells; species, tissue, disease and assay context affect transfer.
  • Strong scores with contradictory markers: investigate preprocessing, doublets, mixed clusters and classes missing from the reference. A classifier still assigns the closest available class in best-match mode.
  • Majority-vote labels erase heterogeneity: compare refined labels with per-cell predictions and the clustering used for refinement. The result depends on over-clustering choices.
  • External processing of sensitive data: keep patient-linked counts, metadata and cell identifiers within approved systems; do not send them to a third-party service without institutional authorization.

    • References and version checks

    The prediction and diagnostic stages completed on 2,638 cells prepared from the official public 10x PBMC 3k counts, using CellTypist 1.7.1, Scanpy 1.12.4 and the official Immune_All_Low.pkl version-2 model on Ubuntu. The query matched 4,177 of the model's 6,639 features; cell-aligned review, probability and decision tables, an annotated H5AD and a completed run manifest were written. This checks software execution, not independent biological label accuracy. The synthetic low-overlap refusal test is retained. The model is loaded by an explicit local path: in CellTypist 1.7.1, a basename can trigger a catalog lookup and download other models even when the named file is present locally. Native Windows/macOS model inference and other datasets remain untested. Record installed versions and recheck APIs, model inventory and defaults before use.

Run tests or validation commands already documented by the project. Do not assume a generic command exists or install new packages just to make an assistant's output appear validated. For scientific code, verify input files, parameters, units, sample identifiers, and outputs against the analysis plan and appropriate controls.

If a command fails, identify whether the cause is a missing dependency, an incorrect path, a code error, or an environment mismatch before asking for a fix. If it passes, record exactly which command ran and on what test data. A passing software test does not validate biological interpretation or establish reproducibility on another platform.

Practice check

Predict the validator result before running it. It should pass only when the single expected sentence is added and both copies remain otherwise untouched. A changed number, missing sentence, extra file, staged edit, or other README wording must be rejected. Then restore the baseline in each copy with git restore README.md and check git status --short is empty. This fixture test is scripted and offline. It does not mean either assistant or a hosted model was run.

Optional next exercise: inspect a synthetic count table

This exercise uses only an invented three-gene by two-sample table. Download the synthetic TSV and standard-library checker into one folder, then run:

python3 inspect_counts.py counts.tsv

Before running it, predict the orientation and sample totals. The first column is gene identifiers, rows are genes and columns are samples. The checker requires a rectangular table with unique identifiers and finite, nonnegative integers, then sums each sample column. The expected column sums are sample_A: 16 and sample_B: 12; the arithmetic total is 28.

Deliberately faulty proposal: “Each row is a sample, so the sample totals are 20, 3, and 5.” Reject it. Those are row sums for genes because the table is genes by samples, not per-sample totals. The correct response is to report the column sums above and explain the orientation.

Answer rubric: identify genes as rows and samples as columns; report 16 and 12 by summing columns; reject negative values, decimals, NaN, and infinity as not nonnegative integer counts; and state that shape, integer, and sum checks do not prove that values are truly raw counts, have correct provenance, preserve sample identity, represent independent samples, or support any biological conclusion. The example is synthetic arithmetic only. Do not infer biology from it.

Verification boundary: the linked helper scripts use only the Python standard library and Git. They were checked locally with Python 3.12.3 and Git 2.43.0. Cursor, Aider, hosted providers, and model responses were not installed or run; no model request or paid call was made.

Choosing between the two tools

Use Cursor when an interactive editor and visual diff review fit your work. Use Aider when a terminal workflow in a Git repository fits better. They can complement each other, but using both does not provide independent scientific validation: both may produce plausible, incorrect changes. Keep analysis design and biological interpretation with the researcher.

The prompt below uses the same input and output locations as the Seurat template: ./data/seurat_obj.rds and ./results/cluster2_markers.csv, plus the cluster-colored UMAP at ./results/umap_seurat_clusters.png.     Goal: Identify marker genes for cluster 2 vs all in a PBMC dataset using the Seurat example below.
Input: RDS Seurat object at ./data/seurat_obj.rds; inspect and report its actual dimensions; metadata column 'seurat_clusters' must be present.
Constraints: Use R and Seurat >=4; test = MAST; logfc.threshold = 0.25; return genes with p_val_adj < 0.05; save a CSV report.
Output: ./results/cluster2_markers.csv and UMAP plot ./results/umap_seurat_clusters.png
Checks: verify the file exists, inspect actual column names and row count (zero rows can be valid), confirm the intended identities were compared, and open the UMAP PNG.
Ask: show all package imports and version prints; explain any assumptions and cite Seurat functions used.

    Reproducible, sequential workflow examples

    The R Seurat workflow below is the main route and implements the cluster-2 marker prompt. The optional Python Scanpy workflow is a separate QC → clustering → exploratory marker-ranking task; it is not an equivalent implementation of the Seurat prompt or a shared sequential pipeline. Both are templates for prepared objects.

    Main workflow: Seurat cluster markers (R)

    Prepare a serialized Seurat object at ./data/seurat_obj.rds, with an RNA expression assay and a seurat_clusters metadata column. Check its structure from the project root before running the workflow:

    Rscript -e 'x <- readRDS("./data/seurat_obj.rds"); print(dim(x)); print(colnames(x@meta.data)); stopifnot("seurat_clusters" %in% colnames(x@meta.data))'

    Expect nonzero feature-by-cell dimensions and the required metadata field. This structural check does not establish that counts, assay choice, identities, or biological annotations are appropriate. If the object or required field is missing, stop and prepare a compatible object first. The existing seurat_clusters labels define the marker comparison; if UMAP is absent, the script computes a visualization without reclustering or replacing those labels.

    • Input Seurat object: ./data/seurat_obj.rds (serialized Seurat object from saveRDS)
    • Output directory: ./results/
    # Save this as ./scripts/seurat_marker_workflow.R
library(Seurat)
library(ggplot2)
library(MAST) # used for statistical test
library(dplyr)
library(tibble) # provides rownames_to_column

# Paths
infile <- "./data/seurat_obj.rds"
outdir <- "./results"
dir.create(outdir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

# Load object and report
seurat_obj <- readRDS(infile)
cat("Seurat object dimensions (cells x genes):", dim(seurat_obj), "\n")
cat("Available metadata columns:", paste(colnames(seurat_obj@meta.data), collapse=", "), "\n")

# Validate metadata before plotting or using the cluster identities.
if (!"seurat_clusters" %in% colnames(seurat_obj@meta.data)) {
  stop("Required metadata column 'seurat_clusters' is missing; prepare or select the intended identities first.")
}

# Record the incoming biological labels and intended marker comparison.
incoming_cluster_labels <- unname(as.character(seurat_obj[[]][["seurat_clusters"]]))
if (anyNA(incoming_cluster_labels)) {
  stop("Required metadata column 'seurat_clusters' contains missing labels.")
}
cluster_of_interest <- "2"
comparison_metadata <- list(
  identity_field = "seurat_clusters",
  cluster_of_interest = cluster_of_interest,
  ident.1 = cluster_of_interest,
  ident.2 = NULL,
  reference = "all other cells",
  test = "MAST",
  assay = DefaultAssay(seurat_obj),
  logfc.threshold = 0.25,
  min.pct = 0.1
)

# Compute a visualization only when missing. Do not call FindClusters here:
# a new clustering would silently replace the required marker-comparison labels.
if (!"umap" %in% names(seurat_obj@reductions)) {
  seurat_obj <- NormalizeData(seurat_obj, verbose = FALSE)
  seurat_obj <- FindVariableFeatures(seurat_obj, selection.method = "vst", nfeatures = 2000, verbose = FALSE)
  seurat_obj <- ScaleData(seurat_obj, verbose = FALSE)
  seurat_obj <- RunPCA(seurat_obj, verbose = FALSE)
  available_pcs <- ncol(Embeddings(seurat_obj, reduction = "pca"))
  if (available_pcs < 2L) {
    stop("At least two PCA dimensions are needed to compute the UMAP visualization.")
  }
  umap_dims <- seq_len(min(20L, available_pcs))
  seurat_obj <- FindNeighbors(seurat_obj, dims = umap_dims, verbose = FALSE)
  seurat_obj <- RunUMAP(seurat_obj, dims = umap_dims, verbose = FALSE)
}

# Visualization work must leave the input biological labels unchanged.
if (!identical(unname(as.character(seurat_obj[[]][["seurat_clusters"]])), incoming_cluster_labels)) {
  stop("The incoming seurat_clusters labels changed while preparing the UMAP.")
}

# Save UMAP plot (colored by clusters)
p <- DimPlot(seurat_obj, reduction = "umap", group.by = "seurat_clusters") + ggtitle("UMAP by seurat_clusters")
ggsave(filename = file.path(outdir, "umap_seurat_clusters.png"), plot = p, width = 6, height = 5)

# Select and persist the explicitly intended comparison metadata.
Idents(seurat_obj) <- comparison_metadata$identity_field
comparison_metadata$observed_identity_labels <- sort(unique(as.character(seurat_obj[[]][["seurat_clusters"]])))
seurat_obj@misc$cluster2_marker_comparison <- comparison_metadata
print(comparison_metadata)

# Exploratory cell-level marker test. For condition-level inference across samples,
# use a sample-aware design rather than treating cells as replicates.
markers <- FindMarkers(seurat_obj,
                       ident.1 = comparison_metadata$ident.1,
                       ident.2 = comparison_metadata$ident.2,
                       assay = comparison_metadata$assay,
                       test.use = comparison_metadata$test,
                       logfc.threshold = comparison_metadata$logfc.threshold,
                       min.pct = comparison_metadata$min.pct)

# Filter by adjusted p-value
significant_markers <- markers %>% rownames_to_column(var = "gene") %>% filter(p_val_adj < 0.05)
write.csv(significant_markers, file = file.path(outdir, paste0("cluster", cluster_of_interest, "_markers.csv")), row.names = FALSE)

# Save computed reductions, unchanged incoming labels, and comparison metadata.
saveRDS(seurat_obj, file = file.path(outdir, "seurat_obj_processed.rds"))
message("Wrote results to ", outdir)

    What each command produces:

    • ./results/umap_seurat_clusters.png: UMAP colored by 'seurat_clusters'.
    • ./results/cluster2_markers.csv: exploratory differential-expression results for cluster 2 versus the remaining cells, filtered by adjusted p-value.
    • ./results/seurat_obj_processed.rds: Seurat object with any computed reductions, unchanged incoming cluster labels, and the recorded cluster-2 comparison metadata.

    Optional Python route: the following uses a separate AnnData input and performs its own QC and clustering; do not compare its outputs as if they came from the same preprocessing or marker-test contract as the Seurat analysis.

    Optional, distinct workflow: Scanpy QC and exploratory markers (Python)

    Prepare an AnnData file at ./data/adata.h5ad with gene symbols in var_names and count-like values in .X; this template computes QC metrics but does not create the object. From the project root, check the input before running the workflow:

    python -c "import scanpy as sc; a=sc.read_h5ad('./data/adata.h5ad'); print(a.shape); print(list(a.obs.columns)); print(a.var_names[:5].tolist())"

    Confirm that the printed dimensions are nonzero, feature names are the expected organism-specific identifiers, and .X contains the intended count-like data. If the file is absent or the structure is different, stop and prepare or locate a compatible object rather than proceeding.

    The Seurat script saves the incoming seurat_clusters vector, makes only a PCA/neighbor/UMAP visualization, checks that the vector is unchanged, then records identity_field = "seurat_clusters", ident.1 = "2", and ident.2 = NULL (all other cells). What you will build

A small orchestrator coordinates a planner, input validator, tool executor, and numerical reviewer. It checks count-table structure, computes sample-level QC, optionally calculates descriptive counts per million (CPM), records provenance, and stops for human review.

  • Prerequisites: basic Python, CSV files, and terminal commands.
  • Offline path: Python 3.10 or later; no packages, API key, network request, or paid model call is required.
  • Optional AI path: one model call proposes an allowlisted JSON plan. It cannot write or run arbitrary code.
  • Success: reproduce known toy results, trigger deliberate failures safely, and explain why passing software checks is not biological validation.

This is not an autonomous scientist. The default run is a deterministic, role-based teaching simulation, not a team of AI agents. The optional planner adds an actual language-model call, but the execution and review remain ordinary Python. This distinction lets you test orchestration mechanics before introducing model variability.

For a broader introduction to agent frameworks, read Advanced Orchestration: Agent Frameworks & Foundation Models. This lesson is different: its focus is a complete small workflow with files, checks, and reproducible outcomes.

What you will build

A small, bounded local R workflow validates a count matrix and matching sample metadata, computes sample-level quality summaries, optionally calculates descriptive counts per million (CPM), records input and script provenance, and stops for human review.

  • Prerequisites: basic terminal and CSV experience, plus R 4.0 or later.
  • Offline path: base R only. No package installation, account, API key, network request, or paid call is needed.
  • Success: reproduce the supplied synthetic results, trigger a deliberate zero-library failure safely, and explain why software checks are not biological validation.

This R implementation is deterministic local code, not an autonomous scientist or an AI planner. It has a fixed allowlist of QC and CPM steps; it does not call a language model, execute generated code, remove samples, or infer research conclusions. The original Python workflow is retained below as an optional alternative, including its separate optional provider demonstration.

On this page
  1. Download the R workflow and tests
  2. Inspect the matching synthetic inputs
  3. Run QC and read the output
  4. Run CPM and inspect a safe failure
  5. Run the R tests and review provenance
  6. Optional existing Python workflow

1. Download and set up the R workflow

Save the R workflow and its test file in the same new folder. Both use base R and are intended to run locally on the public synthetic fixtures. The R implementation writes the same main result names and QC/CPM columns as the retained Python example, but its manifest identifies files with base R's MD5 function. MD5 is a change-detection identifier here, not a security or authenticity guarantee.

  • Download orchestrator_workflow.R
  • Download test_orchestrator_workflow.R
R --version
Rscript orchestrator_workflow.R --help

If Rscript is missing, install R from CRAN. No R packages are required. Keep the offline exercise separate from real research data until you understand its limits.

2. Inspect the matching synthetic inputs

Rscript orchestrator_workflow.R --make-demo demo

This creates counts.csv, counts_positive.csv, and metadata.csv with the same values and headers as the existing Python workflow. The values are invented for teaching, not patient data or a downloaded GEO study. The output folder must not already exist.

gene_id,S1,S2,S3
GENE1,10,20,0
GENE2,0,5,0
GENE3,90,75,0
GENE4,0,0,0

The metadata header is exactly sample_id,group. The input validator requires matching unique sample IDs, simple identifiers, rectangular rows, and nonnegative integer counts. Metadata rows may be reordered because groups are joined by sample ID. This small implementation has explicit training limits of 2 MiB per file, 10,000 genes, and 100 samples; those are software limits, not biological thresholds.

3. Run QC and read the result

Rscript orchestrator_workflow.R --counts demo/counts.csv --metadata demo/metadata.csv --out run-qc

Open run-qc/sample_qc.csv and run-qc/report.md. The three sample totals should be S1: 100, S2: 100, and S3: 0; detected-gene counts are 2, 3, and 0. The default low-library warning threshold of 50 is only an exercise setting. It does not remove samples and is not a recommended RNA-seq cutoff. A zero-count sample is a valid QC input, but its source needs human investigation.

4. Run CPM and inspect the deliberate failure

Use the positive-control fixture for a successful descriptive CPM run:

Rscript orchestrator_workflow.R --counts demo/counts_positive.csv --metadata demo/metadata.csv --out run-cpm --task normalize

Each nonzero sample column in cpm.csv should sum to approximately one million. This is simple column-total scaling, not TPM, composition-bias correction, differential expression, or evidence of a biological effect.

Now request CPM for the fixture with an all-zero S3 column:

Rscript orchestrator_workflow.R --counts demo/counts.csv --metadata demo/metadata.csv --out run-zero-failure --task normalize

The command must fail with a nonzero status because dividing by a zero library total is undefined. It preserves the QC output and a failure event, but must not create cpm.csv or a successful report. Never invent replacement counts to make a real sample pass.

5. Run tests and inspect provenance

Rscript test_orchestrator_workflow.R orchestrator_workflow.R

The tests check the shared demo schema, known QC values, metadata reordering, valid CPM, zero-library refusal, invalid counts and metadata, overwrite protection, and provenance output. Each output directory records a fixed local plan in plan.json, input and script content identifiers and R version in manifest.json, and status events in events.jsonl. A completed report ends at NEEDS_HUMAN_REVIEW. A hash identifies bytes; it does not establish source authenticity, dataset suitability, or scientific correctness.

Inspect files, units, sample identities, warnings, and study design before interpreting any real dataset. The workflow is not a security sandbox, a production pipeline, or an independent biological reviewer. Its calculations are descriptive, and software tests do not validate a research conclusion.

tutorials/autonomous-research-orchestrat.before:
• Output directory already exists: choose a new run name. Do not delete prior evidence just to make a rerun pass.
  • Counts rejected: check for missing fields, duplicate identifiers, non-integer values, or negative counts. Confirm you exported raw counts, not transformed expression.
  • Sample mismatch: compare identifiers exactly. Reordering metadata is allowed; inventing or silently dropping samples is not.
  • Zero-library normalization failure: inspect the original data and QC warning. Do not add artificial counts merely to bypass the check.
  • Optional provider failure: verify the SDK, model ID, account access, environment configuration, and schema support. Return to a clearly labeled offline run rather than silently treating it as AI output.

Practice with an observable result

  1. Reorder the three metadata rows in a copy. Rerun QC into a new directory. Sample identities and metrics should remain the same.
  2. Create a plan file containing {"steps":["qc","run_shell"]} and supply it with --plan blocked-plan.json. The plan must be rejected before tool execution.
  3. Add a duplicate gene or a fractional count to a copied input. Explain which validator rejects it and why silently coercing the value would be unsafe.
  4. Compare two offline runs of unchanged inputs. Match their hashes and numerical outputs; distinguish reproducibility of computation from validity of interpretation.
Check your understanding

Why can QC succeed when S3 has zero counts? Computing and flagging the zero total is valid; normalizing by that total is not. Does a valid model plan establish scientific correctness? No. It establishes only that the proposed tool sequence satisfies the local contract. What is the human approval point? Reviewing the evidence before using or reporting an analysis conclusion; the script never declares that approval on your behalf.

References and further learning

  • Python CSV documentation: file parsing and its explicit conversion requirements.
  • Python argparse documentation: CLI options, validation, and mutually exclusive arguments.
  • OpenAI structured-output guidance: schemas, refusals, and incomplete responses; a schema is not a substitute for application validation.
  • edgeR CPM reference: descriptive CPM and the distinction between simple matrix column sums and normalized library sizes.

tutorials/autonomous-research-orchestrat.after:
• Output directory already exists: choose a new run name. Do not delete prior evidence just to make a rerun pass.
  • Counts rejected: check for missing fields, duplicate identifiers, non-integer values, or negative counts. Confirm you exported raw counts, not transformed expression.
  • Sample mismatch: compare identifiers exactly. Reordering metadata is allowed; inventing or silently dropping samples is not.
  • Zero-library normalization failure: inspect the original data and QC warning. Do not add artificial counts merely to bypass the check.
  • Optional provider failure: verify the SDK, model ID, account access, environment configuration, and schema support. Return to a clearly labeled offline run rather than silently treating it as AI output.

Practice with an observable result

  1. Reorder the three metadata rows in a copy. Rerun QC into a new directory. Sample identities and metrics should remain the same.
  2. Create a plan file containing {"steps":["qc","run_shell"]} and supply it with --plan blocked-plan.json. The plan must be rejected before tool execution.
  3. Add a duplicate gene or a fractional count to a copied input. Explain which validator rejects it and why silently coercing the value would be unsafe.
  4. Compare two offline runs of unchanged inputs. Match their hashes and numerical outputs; distinguish reproducibility of computation from validity of interpretation.

Check your understanding

Why can QC succeed when S3 has zero counts? Computing and flagging the zero total is valid; normalizing by that total is not. Does a valid model plan establish scientific correctness? No. It establishes only that the proposed tool sequence satisfies the local contract. What is the human approval point? Reviewing the evidence before using or reporting an analysis conclusion; the script never declares that approval on your behalf.

References and further learning

  • Python CSV documentation: file parsing and its explicit conversion requirements.
  • Python argparse documentation: CLI options, validation, and mutually exclusive arguments.
  • OpenAI structured-output guidance: schemas, refusals, and incomplete responses; a schema is not a substitute for application validation.
  • edgeR CPM reference: descriptive CPM and the distinction between simple matrix column sums and normalized library sizes.

# Optional summary, if seqkit is installed seqkit stats reads_R1.fastq.gz

In the conventional FASTQ layout, each record has a header beginning with @, a sequence, a + separator, and a quality string of matching length. A nonzero line-count remainder is a warning, not a complete parser-level validation. This quick check assumes unwrapped four-line records; malformed wrapping can invalidate that assumption. pipefail makes a decompression failure visible through the pipeline status in common shells such as Bash.

For paired-end data, compare record counts and read-name identifiers in R1 and R2. Equal counts alone do not show that mates are in the same order or correctly paired. The following Bash/Python check reads both gzip-compressed files in lockstep, verifies four-line records and equal sequence/quality lengths, and compares the first header token after removing a terminal /1 or /2. It assumes the remaining token is identical between mates; if your provider uses a different naming convention (for example, mate labels in a second header field), inspect its documentation and adapt the normalization rather than accepting a mismatch blindly.

python3 - reads_R1.fastq.gz reads_R2.fastq.gz <<'PY'
import gzip, itertools, sys

raise SystemExit(f"FAIL: mate identifiers/order differ at record {n}: {a!r} vs {b!r}") print(f"PASS: {n} paired records; normalized identifiers match in order" if n else "PASS: both files are empty") PY

A PASS establishes only that the parsed records have matching normalized identifiers in order under the stated convention; it does not establish sample identity or biological validity. Any malformed record, count difference, or identifier mismatch stops the check with the first location to investigate. This small Python check assumes readable gzip inputs; adapt the opener for uncompressed FASTQ. Do not treat quality scores as comparable across files until the encoding and instrument/pipeline provenance are known.

CITE-seq measures RNA and antibody-derived tags (ADTs) in the same cells. This template follows the two assays from matched count matrices through separate preprocessing, a Seurat weighted-nearest-neighbor (WNN) graph, and checks that help you interpret modality weights without treating them as biological truth.

Format: Advanced template. For readers familiar with R and single-cell analysis, this adaptable workflow builds and inspects a WNN Seurat object from paired RNA and ADT count matrices you prepare; no dataset is bundled.

Checked route: the five displayed R stages ran on the first 1,000 paired cells from the official CBMC RNA/ADT matrices, using Ubuntu 24.04, R 4.3.3 and Seurat 5.0.1. The example retained 999 cells, produced 12 PCs from 13 ADT features, completed WNN and generated all five PNGs with opaque white backgrounds. This is a bounded software check, not a full-cohort benchmark, biological validation, clean installation test or cross-platform result. Thresholds and dimension caps still need study-specific justification.

A plot can reveal a pattern in an assay, but its appearance depends on preprocessing, model assumptions, and the samples included. This walkthrough follows common QC, sample-structure, expression-pattern, and differential-expression plots, with emphasis on what each view can and cannot support.

Format: Hands-on lab. Learners with basic Python and tabular-data familiarity will generate and inspect QC, PCA, UMAP and heatmap outputs from supplied synthetic tables; a separate R example uses a supplied synthetic DE-style table. No biological data are supplied or analyzed.

Start with the question and the data contract

Choose a plot to answer a defined question. Distributions help compare per-sample QC metrics; PCA summarizes major linear variation among samples; UMAP emphasizes neighborhood structure in a chosen feature space; a heatmap displays selected values across genes and samples; and a volcano plot combines an effect estimate with an adjusted significance measure from a differential-expression analysis.

  • Use sample-level QC values with one row per sample and columns such as sample, batch, condition, total_reads, pct_mt, and mapping_rate. Confirm whether percentages are stored as 5.2 or 0.052 before labeling the axis.
  • For the expression examples, counts.tsv has gene IDs in its first column and one sample per remaining column. Its sample names must match the QC table. Use non-negative raw counts for a count-based differential-expression method; a visualization transform such as log-CPM is not a replacement for that method's input contract.
  • Examples write into results/, which must exist first. Replace example paths with yours. These snippets are recipes, not evidence that any biological dataset was analyzed here.

Run the synthetic lab. Download qc_metrics.tsv, counts.tsv, and (for the separate volcano example) deseq2_results.tsv. These invented teaching values are not biological observations or results from a fitted DESeq2 model. In a new project directory, create data/ and results/ with mkdir -p data results; save the first two downloads as data/qc_metrics.tsv and data/counts.tsv. The count fixture has 10 genes and six samples (S01–S06), and the QC table has one row for each same sample. From the project directory, check Python with python3 --version and python3 -m pip --version; create an isolated environment with python3 -m venv .venv, activate it with source .venv/bin/activate (Windows PowerShell: .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1), then install the Python dependencies with python -m pip install pandas numpy matplotlib seaborn scikit-learn umap-learn. Run each Python block below in order from this project directory (or save each as a script and run python script_name.py). The examples produce the two QC plots, PCA coordinates and plot, UMAP coordinates and plot, and heatmap in results/. Stop if a validation check fails or an expected file is absent; first verify the working directory, paths, columns, and sample IDs. Capture actual installed versions with python -m pip freeze rather than assuming versions.

The volcano block is optional and independent: it needs R and ggplot2 and plots a DE-style results table; it does not run differential-expression analysis. Save the third download as results/deseq2_results.tsv, install ggplot2 if needed with install.packages("ggplot2"), and run the R block from the project directory. It should write results/volcano.png. In real work, use results from a documented model and contrast, not this fixture. Record R.version.string and packageVersion("ggplot2").

Success check: verify six QC rows, six matching count columns, and six sample rows in each coordinate TSV; confirm the QC, PCA, UMAP, heatmap, and (if run) volcano images exist. The synthetic volcano table deliberately has one missing adjusted p-value, which the code filters; inspect and report exclusions rather than interpreting the toy plot biologically.

Record sample count, filtering, normalization or transformation, scaling, plotting parameters, software versions, and any exclusions with each figure. QC thresholds depend on assay and protocol; do not apply a universal cutoff just because it makes a plot cleaner.

Inspect distributions before reducing dimensions

Plot points as well as summaries where the number of samples permits. A boxplot can conceal group size, overlapping observations, or a single unusual sample. The Python snippet reads a tab-separated QC table and compares mitochondrial fraction across batches; the companion histogram shows sequencing depth in millions.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

A plot can reveal a pattern in an assay, but its appearance depends on preprocessing, model assumptions, and the samples included. This R-first walkthrough uses an R Markdown report to create and interpret common QC, sample-structure, expression-pattern, and differential-expression plots, with Python alternatives for the same plotting tasks.

Format: Hands-on lab. Learners with basic R and tabular-data familiarity will render a supplied R Markdown report and inspect QC, PCA, UMAP, heatmap, and volcano-plot outputs from synthetic tables. Python is available as an alternative for each plotting task. No biological data are supplied or analyzed.

Start with the question and the data contract

Choose a plot to answer a defined question. Distributions help compare per-sample QC metrics; PCA summarizes major linear variation among samples; UMAP emphasizes neighborhood structure in a chosen feature space; a heatmap displays selected values across genes and samples; and a volcano plot combines an effect estimate with an adjusted significance measure from a differential-expression analysis.

  • Use sample-level QC values with one row per sample and columns such as sample, batch, condition, total_reads, pct_mt, and mapping_rate. Confirm whether percentages are stored as 5.2 or 0.052 before labeling the axis.
  • For the expression examples, counts.tsv has gene IDs in its first column and one sample per remaining column. Its sample names must match the QC table. Use non-negative raw counts for a count-based differential-expression method; a visualization transform such as log-CPM is not a replacement for that method's input contract.
  • Examples write into results/, which must exist first. Replace example paths with yours. These snippets are recipes, not evidence that any biological dataset was analyzed here.

Run the R Markdown lab

  1. Download the files. Get the R Markdown report, QC table, count table, and DE-style results table. All three tables contain invented teaching values, not biological observations or results from a fitted DESeq2 model.
  2. Set up the project. Place the report at the project root. In an R console, create folders with dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE) and dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE). Save the QC and count tables as data/qc_metrics.tsv and data/counts.tsv; save the DE-style table as results/deseq2_results.tsv. The count fixture has 10 genes and six samples (S01–S06), matched to six QC rows.
  3. Install the R packages once, if needed. Rendering requires rmarkdown and knitr; plots use ggplot2 and uwot. In R, run install.packages(c("rmarkdown", "ggplot2", "uwot")). This report does not install packages automatically.
  4. Check Pandoc after installing those packages. RStudio includes Pandoc. With standalone R, run Rscript -e 'rmarkdown::pandoc_available()'; it should report TRUE. If it reports FALSE, install Pandoc using the official installation guide, then check again.
  5. Render the report. From the project directory, run Rscript -e 'rmarkdown::render("data-visualization-fundamentals.Rmd", output_dir = "results")', or open the file in RStudio and choose Knit. The report checks inputs, writes figures and sample coordinates under results/, and stops if key assumptions fail. Verify the report, figures, and coordinate tables exist. The R panels below can also be run individually from the project root.

The R and Python panels use the same synthetic inputs and address the same plotting task, but software defaults and implementations can change numerical coordinates, clustering order, or visual layout. Treat them as equivalent learning examples, not coordinate-by-coordinate reproductions.

Optional Python setup for the alternative panels

From the project directory, create an environment with python3 -m venv .venv and activate it with source .venv/bin/activate (Windows PowerShell: .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1). Install the plotting dependencies with python -m pip install numpy pandas matplotlib seaborn scikit-learn umap-learn. Run the Python panels from the project root; they use the same synthetic TSV files and plotting tasks as the R examples.

The volcano example only plots a DE-style results table; it does not run differential-expression analysis. In real work, use results from a documented model and contrast, not this fixture. The report includes visible R and package-version output.

Success check: verify six QC rows, six matching count columns, and six sample rows in each coordinate TSV; confirm the QC, PCA, UMAP, heatmap, and volcano images exist. The synthetic volcano table deliberately has one missing adjusted p-value, which the code filters; inspect and report exclusions rather than interpreting the toy plot biologically.

Record sample count, filtering, normalization or transformation, scaling, plotting parameters, software versions, and any exclusions with each figure. QC thresholds depend on assay and protocol; do not apply a universal cutoff just because it makes a plot cleaner.

Inspect distributions before reducing dimensions

Plot points as well as summaries where the number of samples permits. A boxplot can conceal group size, overlapping observations, or a single unusual sample. The R example reads a tab-separated QC table and compares mitochondrial fraction across batches; the companion histogram shows sequencing depth in millions. The Python panel performs the same two descriptive plots.

R

library(ggplot2)
qc <- read.delim("data/qc_metrics.tsv", check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
required <- c("sample", "batch", "condition", "total_reads", "pct_mt")
missing <- setdiff(required, names(qc))
if (length(missing)) stop("QC table is missing columns: ", paste(missing, collapse = ", "))
if (anyNA(qc$sample) || anyDuplicated(qc$sample)) stop("Expected one non-missing QC row per sample")
for (column in c("total_reads", "pct_mt")) {
  qc[[column]] <- as.numeric(qc[[column]])
  bad <- is.na(qc[[column]]) | !is.finite(qc[[column]])
  if (any(bad)) stop("Invalid ", column, " for samples: ", paste(qc$sample[bad], collapse = ", "))
}

qc_boxplot <- ggplot(qc, aes(x = batch, y = pct_mt, color = condition)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(group = batch), outlier.shape = NA, color = "#52616B") +
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.12, dodge.width = 0.75),
             alpha = 0.75, size = 2) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(x = "Batch", y = "Mitochondrial reads (%)",
       title = "Mitochondrial fraction by batch", color = "Condition") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
ggsave("results/qc_boxplot.png", qc_boxplot, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
print(qc_boxplot)

qc_histogram <- ggplot(qc, aes(x = total_reads / 1e6)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 5, fill = "#2C7FB8", color = "white") +
  labs(x = "Total reads (millions)", y = "Samples",
       title = "Sequencing depth") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
ggsave("results/qc_histogram.png", qc_histogram, width = 6, height = 4, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
print(qc_histogram)

The code reports missing, non-numeric, or non-finite values with affected sample IDs. The boxplot shows individual observations; the histogram summarizes a distribution and cannot identify which sample is an outlier. Follow an apparent extreme back to the QC table by sample ID and inspect library size, units, and provenance. With very small groups, treat the histogram/KDE shape as descriptive only. These checks do not decide whether a sample passes QC, and metric names do not define assay-specific thresholds.

PCA: summarize broad sample variation

PCA expects observations in rows and features in columns. Here rows become samples and columns genes. The example computes a simple log2-CPM transform, filters genes by a stated variance rule, then standardizes each retained gene across samples. That last choice gives low-variance genes similar scale to high-variance genes and can amplify noise; it is an exploratory choice, not a universal RNA-seq recommendation. Compare with a suitable variance-stabilizing transform and/or without feature-wise scaling for the assay and question at hand.

The cutoff of 0.01 below retains five of the ten genes in the supplied synthetic count table. A cutoff of 0.5 retains none, so there would be no matrix to plot or pass to UMAP. This small-fixture setting teaches the handoff; it is not a recommended threshold for a biological dataset. Inspect the variance distribution and justify feature selection for real data.

PCA expects observations in rows and features in columns. Here rows become samples and columns genes. R and scikit-learn use slightly different standard-deviation conventions; component signs are arbitrary, so coordinates can differ or appear mirrored without changing the underlying interpretation. R

library(ggplot2)
counts <- read.delim("data/counts.tsv", row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE)
qc <- read.delim("data/qc_metrics.tsv", check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
if (anyDuplicated(rownames(counts)) || anyDuplicated(colnames(counts))) {
  stop("Gene IDs and sample IDs must be unique")
}
counts <- as.matrix(counts)
if (!is.numeric(counts) || any(!is.finite(counts)) || any(counts < 0)) {
  stop("Counts must be finite, numeric, and non-negative")
}
if (any(colSums(counts) == 0)) stop("A sample has zero library size")
if (anyNA(qc$sample) || anyDuplicated(qc$sample)) stop("QC sample IDs must be unique and non-missing")
if (!setequal(colnames(counts), qc$sample)) {
  stop("Counts and QC sample IDs differ; check both tables before plotting")
}
qc <- qc[match(colnames(counts), qc$sample), , drop = FALSE]
if (!identical(qc$sample, colnames(counts))) stop("Could not align QC metadata to count-matrix sample order")

logcpm <- log2(sweep(counts, 2, colSums(counts), "/") * 1e6 + 1)
variances <- apply(logcpm, 1, var)
keep <- variances > 0.01
if (sum(keep) < 2 || ncol(counts) < 2) {
  stop("PCA needs at least two samples and two retained genes")
}
mat <- t(logcpm[keep, , drop = FALSE])
pca <- prcomp(mat, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)
if (ncol(pca$x) < 2) stop("PCA did not return two components for plotting")
explained <- pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2)
pc_scores <- as.data.frame(pca$x)
pc_scores$sample <- rownames(pc_scores)
write.table(pc_scores, "results/pca_full.tsv", sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE)
write.table(pc_scores[, c("sample", "PC1", "PC2")], "results/pca_coords.tsv",
            sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE)

plot_data <- merge(pc_scores, qc[, c("sample", "condition", "batch")], by = "sample", sort = FALSE)
plot_data <- plot_data[match(pc_scores$sample, plot_data$sample), ]
pca_plot <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = condition, shape = batch)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(x = sprintf("PC1 (%.1f%% variance)", 100 * explained[1]),
       y = sprintf("PC2 (%.1f%% variance)", 100 * explained[2]),
       title = "PCA of filtered, scaled log2-CPM", color = "Condition", shape = "Batch") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
ggsave("results/pca_plot.png", pca_plot, width = 6, height = 5, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
print(pca_plot)

The TSVs preserve sample coordinates for later checks. PC1/PC2 percentages describe variance represented by those components under this exact preprocessing. A separation by batch is a cue to inspect design balance, metadata, and possible technical effects; it does not by itself establish a correction method or prove confounding. PCA centers input internally, while the explicit scaler also changes each gene's variance contribution.

UMAP: explore neighborhoods with a specified input

UMAP embeds the rows supplied to it. The example uses all saved PCs available, not the two columns intended for plotting. Small datasets may not support the default neighborhood size, so set n_neighbors below the number of observations and evaluate several sensible settings. n_neighbors changes the local-versus-broader structure considered; min_dist affects how tightly points may pack in the embedding. The coordinates are a visualization, not a calibrated distance scale.

library(ggplot2)
pc_scores <- read.delim("results/pca_full.tsv", check.names = FALSE)

if (!"sample" %in% names(pc_scores) || anyDuplicated(pc_scores$sample)) {

counts <- read.delim("data/counts.tsv", row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE)
counts <- as.matrix(counts)
if (!is.numeric(counts) || any(!is.finite(counts)) || any(counts < 0) || any(colSums(counts) == 0)) {
  stop("Counts must be finite and non-negative, with nonzero library sizes")
}
logcpm <- log2(sweep(counts, 2, colSums(counts), "/") * 1e6 + 1)
variances <- apply(logcpm, 1, var)
top <- names(sort(variances, decreasing = TRUE))[seq_len(min(50, length(variances)))]
selected <- logcpm[top, , drop = FALSE]
row_sd <- apply(selected, 1, function(x) sqrt(mean((x - mean(x))^2)))
selected <- selected[row_sd > 0, , drop = FALSE]
if (anyNA(selected) || nrow(selected) < 2 || ncol(selected) < 2) {
  stop("Need at least two non-constant genes, two samples, and no missing values")
}
z <- t(apply(selected, 1, function(x) (x - mean(x)) / sqrt(mean((x - mean(x))^2))))
row_order <- hclust(dist(z), method = "average")$order
column_order <- hclust(dist(t(z)), method = "average")$order
z_ordered <- z[row_order, column_order, drop = FALSE]
heatmap_data <- as.data.frame(as.table(z_ordered), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
names(heatmap_data) <- c("gene_id", "sample", "z_score")
heatmap_data$gene_id <- factor(heatmap_data$gene_id, levels = rev(rownames(z_ordered)))
heatmap_data$sample <- factor(heatmap_data$sample, levels = colnames(z_ordered))

  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166AC", mid = "white", high = "#B2182B", midpoint = 0) +
  labs(x = "Sample", y = "Gene", fill = "Row z-score",
       title = "Variable genes across samples") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

Volcano plots: display model results, not raw counts

A volcano plot uses differential-expression output. In this DESeq2-style table, log2FoldChange is the estimated effect and padj is the adjusted p-value; missing adjusted values can occur and should not be silently plotted as zero. The thresholds below are illustrative display cutoffs, not universal biological criteria. Do not use this plot as a substitute for checking the model, design, contrasts, and multiple-testing procedure.

library(ggplot2)
res <- read.delim("results/deseq2_results.tsv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
required <- c("log2FoldChange", "padj")
if (!all(required %in% names(res))) stop("Input needs log2FoldChange and padj columns")
res <- res[is.finite(res$log2FoldChange) & !is.na(res$padj) &
             is.finite(res$padj) & res$padj > 0 & res$padj <= 1, ]
res$label <- ifelse(res$padj < 0.05 & abs(res$log2FoldChange) > 1,
                    "passes display cutoffs", "does not pass")
p <- ggplot(res, aes(x = log2FoldChange, y = -log10(padj), color = label)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("does not pass" = "#777777",
                                "passes display cutoffs" = "#B2182B")) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "log2 fold change", y = "-log10 adjusted p-value",
       color = NULL, title = "Differential-expression results") +
  theme_minimal()
ggsave("results/volcano.png", plot = p, width = 6, height = 5, dpi = 300, bg = "white")

Rows with zero adjusted p-values would have an infinite plotted value and are omitted here along with missing values. Report how many rows were omitted and why in a real analysis, especially if filtering or independent filtering produced missing adjusted p-values. A small adjusted p-value can accompany a small effect; statistical evidence and biological importance are separate judgments.

Use plots as diagnostics, then follow up

  • QC shifts: verify metric units, group sizes, and metadata; a batch shift can arise from technical or design differences, but a plot alone cannot identify its cause.
  • PCA separation: inspect the explained variance, sample labels, design balance, and component loadings. Consider the experimental model before choosing batch correction; indiscriminate correction can remove biological signal.
  • Fragmented UMAP: check feature selection, sample count, scaling, and parameter sensitivity. Raising n_neighbors broadens neighborhoods, while changing min_dist changes packing; neither guarantees meaningful clusters.
  • Uniform heatmap: check transformation, selected features, and color limits. Row scaling may reveal relative patterns while hiding absolute amplitude.
  • Volcano extremes: check missing or zero adjusted p-values, effect-size estimates, model formula, contrast, and multiplicity correction before labeling candidates.

Captions should identify the dataset and number of samples, transformation and filtering, encoding and thresholds, package versions, and the main limitation. Use gget to query Ensembl-linked metadata and sequence records, then preserve the raw response and enough provenance to interpret it later. Database retrieval is reproducible only when you record the software, query, source state, and response; an LLM can still misread supplied evidence.

Format: Hands-on lab. This guided exercise is for learners comfortable with a Unix-like shell; you will install pinned gget, retrieve metadata and a protein FASTA for the supplied ACE2 Ensembl ID, and inspect saved outputs. No input files are supplied or needed; an internet connection and package-install permission are required.

Learning objectives and prerequisites

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • Install gget in an isolated Python environment and record the installed version.
  • Retrieve gene metadata and a translated sequence using the documented gget CLI and Python API.
  • Save raw responses and query provenance so a human or LLM can inspect the supplied evidence.
  • Interpret common outputs (IDs, coordinates, sequences) and understand what they do and do not prove.

Prerequisites: basic command-line familiarity (bash or similar), a Python environment supported by your chosen gget release, and permission to install Python packages. No prior knowledge of gget or the Ensembl/UniProt APIs is required.

Why deterministic retrieval matters in bioinformatics

Large Language Models (LLMs) are powerful at synthesizing text and generating code, but they are not authoritative sources of changing biological facts such as current Ensembl gene IDs, transcript coordinates, or canonical UniProt accessions. These facts change over time: annotations are updated, assemblies are remapped, and IDs may be deprecated. Supplying an LLM with a saved database response gives it evidence to inspect, but does not prevent hallucinations or guarantee correct interpretation. Record the query, retrieval time, software version, and relevant database release so another person can assess the result.

gget provides separate command-line and Python modules for querying bioinformatics resources. Here, we use its Ensembl-linked info and seq modules. The query is explicit, but the remote annotation can change between releases; saving the response preserves what you received, not the database service itself.

Reproducible, sequential workflow

The example uses the human ACE2 Ensembl gene ID documented in the gget quick start. Commands assume a Unix-like shell and an internet connection. Gene symbols can be ambiguous; resolve a symbol to the intended Ensembl ID before using this pattern. Responses from external services may change over time.

1) Create an isolated environment and install gget

Run these commands from a new working directory. Create the results directory before redirecting help output:

# Create and activate a Python virtual environment
mkdir -p retrieval-results
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

# Install the direct dependency set exercised in the recorded Linux/Python 3.12.3 run
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install "gget==0.28.6" "numpy==1.26.4" "pandas==2.2.3"

# Verify installation and save the help output
gget --help > retrieval-results/gget-help.txt 2>&1
python -m pip show gget > retrieval-results/gget-package.txt

What these commands produce:

  • .venv/: isolated Python environment (do not delete if you want reproducibility).
  • retrieval-results/gget-help.txt: records the CLI help output.
  • retrieval-results/gget-package.txt: records installed gget package metadata, including its version.

The example pins gget 0.28.6 with NumPy 1.26.4 and pandas 2.2.3, exercised on Linux with Python 3.12.3. An initial install with current unconstrained dependencies failed because this gget release calls np.NaN, removed in NumPy 2. The direct constraints and full observed environment preserve what worked; they are not cross-platform guarantees. Do not silently replace versions when reproducing this run.

2) Prepare a retrieval-results directory and record metadata

# Make a directory to hold raw retrievals and logs
mkdir -p retrieval-results
# Record the environment and Python package list for provenance
python -m pip freeze > retrieval-results/requirements.txt
python --version > retrieval-results/python-version.txt
date -u '+%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ' > retrieval-results/retrieval_timestamp.txt

Files created:

  • retrieval-results/requirements.txt: installed Python distributions, not a complete lockfile of platform dependencies.
  • retrieval-results/retrieval_timestamp.txt: time the environment metadata was captured; it is not a query start or completion time.

3) Deterministic retrieval: get Ensembl gene metadata using gget info

Use an Ensembl gene identifier, not a gene symbol: gget info accepts Ensembl IDs and writes JSON to standard output by default. The official quick start uses ENSG00000130234 for ACE2.

# Log start/end, exact command label, and exit status around each CLI query
log_run() {
  label=$1; shift
  started=$(date -u '+%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ')
  "$@"
  status=$?
  finished=$(date -u '+%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ')
  printf 'start=%s | command=%s | exit=%s | end=%s\n' "$started" "$label" "$status" "$finished" >> retrieval-results/commands.log
  return "$status"
}
# Save the raw command-line JSON; inspect stderr and do not interpret output if it fails
log_run 'gget info ENSG00000130234' gget info ENSG00000130234 > retrieval-results/ACE2_info.json || echo "gget info failed; inspect stderr and output file."

# Python API: info returns a pandas DataFrame; export its returned columns
python - <<'PY'
import gget
records = gget.info(["ENSG00000130234"])
records.to_csv("retrieval-results/ACE2_info_python.csv", index=False)
print("Rows:", len(records), "Columns:", list(records.columns))
PY

The Python call is a separate live query and is not wrapped by the shell logger above. Compare its saved rows with the CLI response, rather than assuming the output fields or source annotations are identical. Keep the raw JSON: a summary table can omit fields needed later.

4) Deterministic retrieval: download a protein sequence with gget seq

Fetch translated sequence output for the same gene. The gget manual states that --translate returns amino-acid sequences fetched from UniProt, while nucleotide sequences are fetched from Ensembl; --isoforms requests sequences for all known transcripts for a gene ID. The manual does not establish a canonical-selection rule for this default query, so identify any accession/isoform from the returned FASTA header and source record rather than assuming which product was selected.

log_run 'gget seq --translate ENSG00000130234' gget seq --translate ENSG00000130234 > retrieval-results/ACE2_protein.fasta || echo "gget seq failed; inspect stderr and output file."

# Structural check: require a FASTA header and at least one sequence character
python - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
p = Path("retrieval-results/ACE2_protein.fasta")
lines = p.read_text().splitlines()
if not lines or not lines[0].startswith(">") or not any(line.strip() for line in lines[1:]):
    raise SystemExit("FAIL: expected a FASTA header followed by a non-empty sequence; inspect the file and gget error before retrying")
print("Header:", lines[0])
print("Sequence characters:", sum(len(line.strip()) for line in lines[1:]))
PY

Illustrative shape only (not a promised ACE2 accession or sequence): >source_record_id description or isoform details followed by one or more lines of amino-acid letters. A header-and-sequence check catches empty files and many error-page responses, but it does not prove the record matches the requested gene. If the check fails, inspect the file beginning and command error, verify network/service availability, and rerun only after resolving the cause. If it passes, compare the header identifier with the relevant UniProt record; report unresolved mapping or isoform identity as unknown.

Files produced:

  • retrieval-results/ACE2_protein.fasta: FASTA output from gget. For translated output, gget uses UniProt; it is not a sequence fetched from Ensembl.

5) Save exact commands, inputs, and timestamps for provenance

The two CLI retrievals above append UTC start and completion timestamps, the exact command labels, and exit statuses to retrieval-results/commands.log. The portable date -u format works with GNU and BSD/macOS date; it does not require GNU's --iso-8601 option. The separate Python API query is not wrapped by this logger. Times bracket execution; they do not freeze upstream database state.

Files produced:

  • retrieval-results/commands.log: UTC start/end timestamps, exact command labels, and exit status for CLI retrievals. These timestamps bracket execution; they do not freeze upstream database state.

Observed example: an actual ACE2 retrieval

On 23 October 2026 UTC, both CLI queries above completed with exit status zero in the constrained environment. They were executed using the downloadable bounded query runner, which saves raw stdout/stderr, versions, hashes and UTC timestamps and refuses an existing results directory. See its reproduction notes and actual run manifest. The separate Python API export above was not part of this recorded run.

Format: Hands-on lab. This guided exercise is for learners comfortable with a Unix-like shell. Use the gget CLI to retrieve gene metadata and translated FASTA for the ACE2 Ensembl ID, then inspect the saved output with R and jsonlite. gget must already be available under its current official instructions; a Python API example is optional. No biological input files are supplied or needed. Live retrieval needs internet access.

Learning objectives and prerequisites

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • Run gget's documented command-line retrievals for an Ensembl gene ID and save the raw JSON and FASTA responses.
  • Use R to inspect the saved CLI outputs without claiming that gget has an R API.
  • Preserve query provenance and assess what the returned records do and do not support.

Prerequisites: basic command-line familiarity, the gget command-line program installed and configured using its current official instructions, an internet connection, and R with the small jsonlite package for JSON parsing. gget's CLI remains the retrieval tool; R reads its saved files. No research data are required. Do not install a new environment or paid service for this lesson unless your local policy permits it.

Why deterministic retrieval matters in bioinformatics

Large Language Models (LLMs) can synthesize text and generate code, but they are not authoritative sources of changing biological facts such as current Ensembl gene IDs, transcript coordinates, or canonical UniProt accessions. Supplying an LLM with a saved database response gives it evidence to inspect, but does not prevent hallucinations or guarantee correct interpretation. Record the query, retrieval time, software version, and relevant database release so another person can assess the result.

gget provides native command-line subcommands for querying bioinformatics resources. The route below uses gget CLI for retrieval, then R only to inspect the saved response. A request made through gget CLI is not the same request or API behavior as a separate gget Python API call. Remote annotations can change between runs; saving the response preserves what you received, not the database service itself.

Reproducible, sequential workflow

The example uses the human ACE2 Ensembl gene ID shown in gget's documented quick start, ENSG00000130234. Commands assume a Unix-like shell and internet access. Gene symbols can be ambiguous; resolve a symbol to an intended Ensembl ID before using this pattern. Responses from external services may change over time.

1) Check the CLI and prepare output files

Start with gget already installed according to its current official documentation. The project does not pin or reinstall Python dependencies for the R inspection route. From a new working directory, create a results folder, check the CLI help and executable path, and record a UTC timestamp:

mkdir -p retrieval-results
if ! command -v gget; then echo "gget CLI is not available; follow its official installation instructions." >&2; exit 127; fi
gget --help > retrieval-results/gget-help.txt 2>&1
printf 'query_start_utc=%s\n' "$(date -u '+%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ')" > retrieval-results/commands.log

The commands create retrieval-results/gget-help.txt and retrieval-results/commands.log. Record the exact gget version using the installation method's documented version/package-inspection command; no version flag is assumed to be portable across releases. If the CLI is missing, follow gget's official installation documentation and check the version and platform compatibility before continuing.

2) Retrieve the gene record and protein FASTA with native gget CLI

Keep the commands explicit and save standard output as raw response files. gget failures should be diagnosed from the command's exit status and standard error before interpreting any partial file.

# Log start/end, exact command label, and exit status around each CLI query
log_run() {
  label=$1; shift
  started=$(date -u '+%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ')
  "$@"
  status=$?
  finished=$(date -u '+%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ')
  printf 'start=%s | command=%s | exit=%s | end=%s\n' "$started" "$label" "$status" "$finished" >> retrieval-results/commands.log
  return "$status"
}
# Save the raw command-line JSON and translated FASTA; stop on a failed query.
if log_run 'gget info ENSG00000130234' gget info ENSG00000130234 > retrieval-results/ACE2_info.json; then
  printf 'gget_info_exit=0\n' >> retrieval-results/commands.log
else
  status=$?
  printf 'gget_info_exit=%s\n' "$status" >> retrieval-results/commands.log
  echo "gget info failed; inspect stderr and the partial output before retrying." >&2
  exit "$status"
fi

if log_run 'gget seq --translate ENSG00000130234' gget seq --translate ENSG00000130234 > retrieval-results/ACE2_protein.fasta; then
  printf 'gget_seq_exit=0\n' >> retrieval-results/commands.log
else
  status=$?
  printf 'gget_seq_exit=%s\n' "$status" >> retrieval-results/commands.log
  echo "gget seq failed; inspect stderr and the partial output before retrying." >&2
  exit "$status"
fi
printf 'query_end_utc=%s\n' "$(date -u '+%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ')" >> retrieval-results/commands.log

retrieval-results/ACE2_info.json holds the raw CLI JSON and retrieval-results/ACE2_protein.fasta holds translated sequence output. The gget manual identifies --translate amino-acid retrieval as coming from UniProt, while nucleotide sequences are fetched from Ensembl. The command itself does not establish a canonical-selection rule: inspect the returned header and source record rather than assuming which isoform was selected. The helper logs UTC start/end times and exit status for each command. This provenance does not freeze upstream database state or identify a database release.

3) Inspect saved CLI JSON and FASTA with R

This primary R utility reads local outputs only; it makes no network request and does not recreate gget. It requires R and jsonlite. Save as inspect_retrieval.R in the same working directory after the CLI files exist, then run Rscript inspect_retrieval.R. The script prints the R and jsonlite versions used for this inspection.

if (!requireNamespace("jsonlite", quietly = TRUE)) {
  stop("Install or load jsonlite according to local policy before parsing JSON")
}
cat("R version:", R.version.string, "\n")
cat("jsonlite version:", as.character(utils::packageVersion("jsonlite")), "\n")
info_path <- "retrieval-results/ACE2_info.json"
if (!file.exists(info_path) || file.info(info_path)$size == 0)
  stop("Missing or empty gget JSON output; inspect the CLI error before retrying")
info <- jsonlite::fromJSON(info_path, simplifyVector = FALSE)
cat("Top-level JSON fields:", paste(names(info), collapse = ", "), "\n")
str(info, max.level = 2)

fasta_path <- "retrieval-results/ACE2_protein.fasta"
if (!file.exists(fasta_path) || file.info(fasta_path)$size == 0)
  stop("Missing or empty FASTA output; inspect the CLI error before retrying")
lines <- readLines(fasta_path, warn = FALSE)
headers <- grep("^>", lines, value = TRUE)
if (!length(headers)) stop("No FASTA header found; inspect the saved file and CLI error")
sequence_lines <- lines[!grepl("^>", lines)]
sequence_length <- sum(nchar(gsub("\\s+", "", sequence_lines, perl = TRUE)))
if (sequence_length == 0L) stop("FASTA header exists but sequence is empty")
cat("FASTA records:", length(headers), "\nFirst header:", headers[[1]],
    "\nSequence characters:", sequence_length, "\n")

Expected result: R prints the JSON top-level field names and a short structure, plus one or more returned FASTA headers and a non-zero character count. A structural pass catches empty files and some error-page responses; it does not prove the record matches the intended gene, validate the sequence, or establish function. Compare the returned identifiers with their source records and report unresolved mapping or isoform identity as unknown.

For a safe offline practice run, create a fresh temporary directory, then create these synthetic fixtures there before running the R script:

mkdir -p /tmp/gget-inspection-fixture/retrieval-results
cd /tmp/gget-inspection-fixture
cat > retrieval-results/ACE2_info.json <<'EOF'
{"id":"SYNTHETIC1","description":"invented test record"}
EOF
cat > retrieval-results/ACE2_protein.fasta <<'EOF'
>SYNTHETIC_PROTEIN invented fixture only
MKT
EOF
# Copy inspect_retrieval.R into this directory first, then run it
Rscript inspect_retrieval.R

The R script tests local file parsing only; the synthetic values are not biological observations. Use a fresh temporary directory and never overwrite a real retrieval directory when practicing.

Optional: gget Python API for Python users

gget also documents a Python API. This is a separate, optional remote request, not an R equivalent and not the same saved response as the CLI query above. Run it only in a compatible Python environment with the version and dependencies required by gget's current documentation. Compare returned fields cautiously; APIs, defaults, and response schemas can differ.

import gget
records = gget.info(["ENSG00000130234"])
records.to_csv("retrieval-results/ACE2_info_python.csv", index=False)
print("Rows:", len(records), "Columns:", list(records.columns))

This Python call sends another query and writes retrieval-results/ACE2_info_python.csv; it is not needed to complete the R-first lesson.

Observed example: an actual ACE2 retrieval

The recorded run used gget==0.28.6, numpy==1.26.4, and pandas==2.2.3. Its direct dependency constraints describe that historical CLI runtime, not universal requirements for R or a recommendation to replace your current environment.

On 23 October 2026 UTC, both CLI queries above completed with exit status zero in the constrained environment. They were executed using the downloadable bounded query runner, which saves raw stdout/stderr, versions, hashes and UTC timestamps and refuses an existing results directory. See its reproduction notes and actual run manifest. The separate Python API export above was not part of this recorded run.

tutorials/evolutionary-phylogeny-analysi.before:
• Familiarity with biological sequence files (FASTA), basic UNIX command line, and the concept of homologous characters and multiple sequence alignment.
  • Access to a Unix-like environment (Linux, macOS, or WSL) with Conda/Mamba or direct binaries for the tools mentioned. The tutorial uses file paths as examples; adapt them to your workspace.

Why evolutionary phylogeny matters (biological and computational context)

Phylogenetic analysis reconstructs relationships among genes, proteins, or organisms by comparing homologous characters (nucleotides or amino acids). Trees summarize hypotheses of shared ancestry: topology (branching pattern) suggests relative relationships, branch lengths often represent estimated genetic change, and support values indicate statistical confidence in clades under the chosen model and data. Phylogenies are used in systematics, comparative genomics, functional inference, and epidemiology, but they are hypotheses, not definitive histories; results depend on the input alignment, model choice, taxon sampling, and methodological assumptions.

To infer phylogenies robustly, perform two main preprocessing steps: (1) generate a reliable MSA that aligns homologous positions across sequences, and (2) choose a phylogenetic method (distance, maximum likelihood, Bayesian, or approximate methods) and explicitly state the evolutionary model and the support strategy (bootstraps, posterior probabilities). This tutorial emphasizes reproducible command-line workflows and careful recording of all settings.

Reproducible workflow (sequential)

Overview: work in a project directory containing raw sequences, intermediate files, configuration files, and results. These examples use paths relative to the project directory. Supply homologous, unaligned sequences in a single FASTA file; records should represent the same locus or a defensible set of orthologous characters, not merely sequences with similar names. Create the results directory before analysis. Validate program flags against installed versions.

Record provenance without overstating reproducibility

Capture the code snapshot used for an analysis after committing the analysis code. The first command writes the current short commit ID; subsequent commands record selected environment details. Because adding these records creates another commit, the saved ID names the code state immediately before the provenance files were committed.

pip3 freeze > requirements.txt
git add COMMIT_HASH.txt ENV_INFO.txt requirements.txt
git commit -m "Record analysis code revision and Python packages"

pip freeze describes installed Python distributions in the active environment. It does not capture R or Bioconductor packages, operating-system libraries, reference genomes, annotation versions, or external databases. Record those separately when they affect the workflow; use a project-appropriate lockfile or container and test the setup on the intended platform.

A Slurm submission script describes the resources a batch job requests and the commands it runs after the scheduler starts it. This walkthrough starts with a small smoke test; later optional examples cover task launches and arrays. Some optional examples use site-specific module names and partition values; confirm any such values with your cluster documentation before adapting or submitting those examples.

Format: Hands-on lab. With an authorized Slurm account and site-specific submission details, learners who have completed Basic Slurm Commands can adapt the harmless batch script, submit it, and inspect its log and final scheduler record. Without cluster access, use the planning check below to practise reading the script and distinguishing an accepted submission from a completed job.

After installation, you can create and manage Conda environments. This allows you to isolate different projects and their dependencies.

conda create --name myenv python=3.8

Activate an environment:

conda activate myenv

Install packages:

conda install numpy pandas

Deactivate an environment:

conda deactivate
