Scope and tested boundary. This lesson evaluates precomputed cell embedding exports; it does not load scGPT/Geneformer weights, run inference, generate embeddings, or infer regulatory networks. The scoring code below is executable offline, but no pretrained model output or biological accuracy claim is supplied. All teaching fixtures are explicitly synthetic.

This is an evaluator for externally generated scGPT or Geneformer embedding exports, not a model-inference tutorial. First, run the deliberately synthetic fixture to check the evaluator and its input contract; then, if you have compatible real exports, evaluate donor-held-out cell-label retrieval. The model-specific sections document the separate upstream handoff and provenance to verify; no pretrained model output is supplied.

Format: Hands-on lab. For learners comfortable running Python from a shell, this lab first uses a generated synthetic CSV fixture as a software check of the linked standard-library evaluator. It then shows how to evaluate your own externally generated scGPT or Geneformer vectors; no model weights, inference, or real embedding exports are included.

On this page

  • Goals and assumptions
  • Model-specific embedding generation handoff
  • Input contract
  • Run the evaluator
  • Read outputs and failure cases
  • Limitations and sources

Goals and assumptions

  • Validate CSV embeddings, dimensions, finite values, and exact cell-ID alignment before comparing labels.
  • Prevent donor overlap between reference and held-out test cells.
  • Run deterministic Euclidean k-nearest-neighbor transfer with disclosed tie handling and top-vote uncertainty; report accuracy, macro-F1, per-class scores, confusion matrix, and donor-level results.
What you will produce. A strict JSON report of nearest-reference predictions and descriptive metrics from supplied vectors, plus an audit trail for the cell-ID join and donor split. The Python evaluator uses only the standard library. It is a small software check, not a replacement for study-specific validation, Scanpy, scIB metrics, or biological review.

Model-specific embedding generation handoff (not executed here)

Use the official implementation and the exact checkpoint’s documented preprocessing to make real embeddings; export one stable cell identifier per row and the corresponding vector with provenance kept separately. Never relabel arbitrary values or synthetic test coordinates as model output.

  • scGPT: its official repository links a reference-mapping tutorial (embed query cells and map against reference embeddings) and an integration tutorial. The model zoo documents distinct checkpoint choices and paired vocabularies; species, gene identifiers, selected checkpoint and the tutorial’s data-preparation conventions must match. The repository describes loading checkpoints via its documented utilities; there is no generic model.encode(adata) API assumed here.
  • Geneformer: the official getting-started docs direct users to install the repository with Git LFS and point to examples for transcriptome tokenization and extracting/plotting cell embeddings. The official examples include tokenizing_scRNAseq_data.ipynb and extract_and_plot_cell_embeddings.ipynb. Follow the selected Geneformer version/checkpoint’s tokenizer, input schema, gene-ID mapping and species expectations; these are not interchangeable with scGPT preprocessing.

Check the actual official notebook and checkpoint/version you will use. Both projects evolve. This lesson intentionally does not claim to have tested either model inference path or provide heavyweight model-install commands. Save model/repository revision, checkpoint identifier/hash, tokenizer/vocabulary, organism, input assay/count conventions, preprocessing, cell-ID mapping, embedding layer/pooling, and export date alongside your vectors.

Input contract

Save two UTF-8 CSV files. The embedding table must have a header with cell_id and one or more embedding_* columns; every subsequent row has exactly one numeric value per dimension. Metadata must have exactly the fields cell_id,donor_id,label,split, with one row per cell. Split must be train (reference) or test. Every donor must occur in one split only. Row ordering may differ because join-by-ID is explicit.

cell_id,embedding_0,embedding_1
ref_001,0.13,-0.28
ref_002,0.07,0.31
test_101,0.22,-0.06
cell_id,donor_id,label,split
ref_001,donor_A,T-cell,train
ref_002,donor_B,B-cell,train
test_101,donor_C,T-cell,test
Split before tuning. These values illustrate the file format only; they are not data or model outputs. Put every cell from a donor in one split. Where the intended claim concerns transfer across sites, studies, or batches, hold out that unit too. Choose the checkpoint, preprocessing, distance metric, k, and thresholds using training/reference-only validation, never the held-out test labels.

Run the evaluator: first a software check, then real embeddings

Download the evaluator and test suite into the same new working folder. The commands below use a macOS/Linux-style shell; Python 3.12 on Linux was tested. The example needs only Python's standard library, not model weights or a GPU.

mkdir embedding-evaluation
cd embedding-evaluation
# Save both downloaded Python files in this folder.
python3 -m unittest -v test_foundation_embedding_workflow.py

A. Reproduce a small, deliberately synthetic software check

The four vectors below are hand-written coordinates, not scGPT or Geneformer outputs. They make the expected nearest-neighbor decisions obvious and let you test the file contract without a model account or download. Their class separation is constructed on purpose; no model-quality or biological result can be inferred from the score.

python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
folder = Path("synthetic_demo")
folder.mkdir()
(folder / "embeddings.csv").write_text(
    "cell_id,embedding_0,embedding_1\n"
    "ref_T,0,0\nref_B,10,10\n"
    "query_T,0.1,0.2\nquery_B,9.8,10.1\n", encoding="utf-8")
(folder / "metadata.csv").write_text(
    "cell_id,donor_id,label,split\n"
    "ref_T,D_reference,T-cell,train\n"
    "ref_B,D_reference,B-cell,train\n"
    "query_T,D_heldout,T-cell,test\n"
    "query_B,D_heldout,B-cell,test\n", encoding="utf-8")
PY
python3 foundation_embedding_workflow.py \
  --embeddings synthetic_demo/embeddings.csv \
  --metadata synthetic_demo/metadata.csv \
  --output synthetic_demo/evaluation.json -k 1

Open synthetic_demo/evaluation.json. The software-check result should contain two test cells: query_T maps to the T-cell reference and query_B to the B-cell reference. Accuracy and macro-F1 are both 1.0 for these deliberately easy toy points only. inference_performed remains false.

Trigger a meaningful failure: copy the metadata file and change a query cell's donor to D_reference. Rerun using that copy and a new output filename. The evaluator must exit with a donor-leakage error and create no evaluation JSON. Reordering rows without changing IDs should not change predictions.

B. Evaluate actual model-exported embeddings

After the software check passes, follow the model-specific handoff above and export your actual vectors. Use the same checkpoint, embedding layer/pooling, dimension ordering, and preprocessing for reference and test cells. Save your real exports as real_embeddings.csv and real_metadata.csv; these are files you must supply, not generated model results included with this lesson.

python3 foundation_embedding_workflow.py \
  --embeddings real_embeddings.csv \
  --metadata real_metadata.csv \
  --output real_evaluation.json -k 3
Before the real-data run: k must be no larger than the number of reference cells (the example uses k=3). Choose k and preprocessing using reference-only validation before examining test labels. Holding donors out in this evaluation does not establish that a pretrained checkpoint never saw those donors or their study during pretraining; check checkpoint training provenance separately.

The tool checks unique headers, rectangular rows, cell-ID agreement, finite coordinates, exact metadata fields, donor separation, valid k, and a fresh output filename. It refuses inputs above 10 MiB per CSV or a comparison budget above 10 million reference-cell × test-cell × embedding-dimension terms. It does not silently subsample. Use an appropriately validated vectorized or nearest-neighbor implementation for larger cohorts, and document any resulting approximation.

Distance overflow produces a scale-review error, not a JSON containing infinity. Output is serialized as strict JSON before exclusive file creation; an existing result is never overwritten. Review the failure message rather than replacing invalid coordinates or leaking held-out labels into a repair.

Read outputs and failure cases

The JSON reports the configuration, split sizes and donors, cell predictions and nearest neighbors, squared Euclidean distances, tie labels, top-vote fraction, confusion matrix, accuracy, macro-F1, per-class precision/recall/F1, and per-test-donor accuracy. Distances depend on the supplied coordinate scale, embedding layer, and preprocessing; compare them only for consistently generated vectors. A tied vote resolves alphabetically and lists all tied labels. The top-vote fraction describes neighbor agreement, not a calibrated probability.

  • Cell-ID mismatch/duplicate: repair upstream barcode/sample prefixes and confirm one-to-one export alignment. Do not “fix” by relying on row order.
  • NaN/infinity or nonnumeric value: trace embedding extraction and CSV serialization; do not silently impute or replace values.
  • Donor leakage: reassign whole donors before exporting metadata. If the scientific target is within-donor generalization, design that validation separately and label it as such.
  • Poor class or donor performance: inspect support and confusion matrix; potential causes include representation failure, shifts in tissue/site/batch, label inconsistency, unrepresented cell state, and class imbalance. Do not tune against held-out test labels.
  • High score: not evidence of biological truth or zero-shot universal transfer. Check marker coherence, independent cohorts, baseline models, batch/site confounding, and annotation quality using a preregistered plan.

Limitations and official sources

This is supervised nearest-neighbor label transfer using labeled reference cells, not zero-shot prediction. Donor exclusion limits a common leakage route but cannot remove confounding when labels align with site, protocol, or disease cohort. A single donor-level split is not a population-level uncertainty estimate. Report cohort composition, per-class support, donor/site performance, baselines, preprocessing, chosen k, and independent replication. No test accuracy is asserted by this tutorial.

Embedding similarity is not a gene-regulatory network, causal edge, differential expression result, or mechanistic claim. Network inference requires separate methods and evidence; no GRN is produced here.

  • Official scGPT repository: model zoo, checkpoints/vocabulary and tutorials.
  • Official scGPT reference mapping notebook.
  • Official Geneformer getting started docs.
  • Official Geneformer examples on Hugging Face: tokenization and cell embedding examples.

Scope and tested boundary. This lesson evaluates supplied, precomputed cell embeddings. It does not load scGPT or Geneformer weights, run inference, generate embeddings, or infer regulatory networks. The included coordinates and labels are deliberately synthetic software-check data, not model outputs or biological evidence.

Use base R to validate embedding and metadata CSVs, align rows by cell ID, reject donor leakage, and evaluate donor-held-out cell-label transfer with squared-Euclidean k-nearest neighbors. The same question can be evaluated with the optional existing Python workflow. Model-specific embedding generation remains an upstream, separately documented step.

Format: Hands-on lab. R is the main route and uses only base R for local evaluation. R Markdown is an optional report wrapper. The only network operation in the companion files is the explicit protein-database retrieval lesson, not this evaluator.

  • Goal and assumptions
  • Upstream embedding handoff

Goal and assumptions

  • Check the exact CSV schema, unique cell identifiers, one-to-one identifier coverage, numeric finite coordinates, and metadata labels.
  • Keep all cells from each donor in one split and reject overlap between the reference and held-out test sets.
  • Run deterministic squared-Euclidean kNN; report accuracy, macro-F1, per-class F1, donor accuracy, neighbor IDs, distances, and top-vote fraction.
What you will produce. One predictions CSV and one metrics CSV. The top-vote fraction is neighbor agreement, not a calibrated probability. This is a small exact evaluator for teaching and modest tables, not a replacement for study-specific validation, Scanpy, scIB metrics, or biological review.

Upstream embedding handoff (not executed here)

Real model vectors must be generated separately with the exact official implementation, checkpoint, tokenizer/vocabulary, organism, preprocessing, embedding layer, and pooling documented for that model. Keep a record of those choices and the export provenance. Do not label toy vectors as scGPT or Geneformer output.

  • scGPT: use the official reference-mapping tutorial or integration tutorial. Check the chosen checkpoint and paired vocabulary and follow its actual preprocessing instructions; this lesson assumes no generic model API.
  • Geneformer: follow its official getting-started documentation and tokenization and embedding examples. Tokenization, gene identifiers, species, model version, and checkpoint differ from scGPT.

No pretrained output, model weights, inference code, GPU requirement, or heavyweight model installation is included or tested here. Donor holdout in this evaluator does not establish that a checkpoint never saw those donors or their study during pretraining.

Input contract

Use two UTF-8 comma-separated files. The embeddings file has a cell_id column followed by one or more embedding_* numeric columns. Metadata has exactly cell_id,donor_id,label,split, with split equal to train or test. Each identifier appears exactly once in each file; row order may differ because the evaluator joins by ID. Donors must be exclusive to one split.

cell_id,embedding_0,embedding_1
ref_T,0,0
ref_B,10,10
query_T,0.1,0.2
query_B,9.8,10.1
cell_id,donor_id,label,split
query_B,heldout_2,B-cell,test
ref_B,reference_2,B-cell,train
ref_T,reference_1,T-cell,train
query_T,heldout_1,T-cell,test

These example rows are a deliberately easy constructed fixture. Their separation and score are software-check facts only. Choose the split unit, checkpoint, preprocessing, distance metric, and k using reference-only validation, never held-out labels.

Run the evaluator: R main route, Python optional

Download evaluate_embeddings.R, the synthetic embedding fixture, and the matching metadata fixture into one new working folder. The R script needs base R only. The adjacent Python command is a complete optional implementation of the same held-out kNN task; download foundation_embedding_workflow.py into that folder to use it.

Rscript evaluate_embeddings.R synthetic_embeddings.csv synthetic_metadata.csv demo 1
python3 foundation_embedding_workflow.py --embeddings synthetic_embeddings.csv --metadata synthetic_metadata.csv --output demo.json -k 1

The R route writes demo_predictions.csv and demo_metrics.csv; the Python route writes a JSON report with the same core accuracy, macro-F1, per-class F1, and donor-level accuracy plus a confusion matrix and detailed per-cell neighbor information. Both runs use identical synthetic rows and are deliberately easy software checks: the two query cells map to constructed labels, with accuracy and macro-F1 of 1.0 only for this toy fixture. Neither computes model embeddings or supports biological claims.

Both evaluators reject donor leakage, mismatched IDs, invalid numeric values, and oversized inputs. The R script refuses CSVs above 10 MiB and comparison workloads above 10 million reference-cell × test-cell × dimension terms; it does not subsample. The Python workflow applies the same teaching limits. Use a fresh result path. The Python test file constructs its own small fixtures; download test_foundation_embedding_workflow.py beside the Python utility and run python3 -m unittest -v test_foundation_embedding_workflow.py.

For the optional report, download foundation_embedding_evaluation.Rmd beside the R script and fixtures. Render with Rscript -e 'rmarkdown::render("foundation_embedding_evaluation.Rmd")' from that directory; rendering requires the rmarkdown package and Pandoc, but the evaluator itself does not.

Interpret results and limitations

Inspect support and misclassified labels, per-class and donor-level metrics, and nearest neighbors before drawing conclusions. Performance may reflect tissue, site, batch, class balance, inconsistent labels, checkpoint exposure, or representation behavior. A high score is not evidence of biological truth, universal transfer, or causal regulation. Check marker coherence, independent cohorts, appropriate baselines, and annotation quality under a prespecified validation plan.

These implementations perform exact neighbor search and are intended for modest teaching tables; they do not tune hyperparameters, calibrate probabilities, calculate integration metrics, test checkpoint pretraining exposure, or verify upstream model provenance. The R CSV outputs and Python JSON output are different report formats. Use only real vectors from a documented upstream model workflow for scientific analysis.

The H5 reader requires hdf5r in the active R library. Install it with install.packages("hdf5r") if missing, then confirm it loads before this branch. Python's normalization and highly-variable-gene selection and Seurat's SCTransform are alternative preprocessing choices; they are not identical transformations or numerically interchangeable. Inspect object and assay/layer names when adapting to another release. If loading fails, confirm the selected directory directly contains filtered_feature_bc_matrix.h5 and spatial/. For your own Space Ranger run this is usually outs/; the prepared public sample uses the named directory above. If counts load without an image, inspect the spatial assets and library metadata before interpreting plots.

Before plotting: confirm that observations and genes are present, the intended tissue image is attached, and coordinates align with that image. Check the feature names in the object; gene-symbol capitalization and assay/layer selection can make a biologically plausible marker appear absent. Stop if the object has zero observations/features, coordinates are missing, or spot positions do not overlay the tissue; resolve input/library mismatches rather than interpreting a coordinate-only scatter as image validation.

2. Plot a feature against tissue context

First plot a basic library-size QC measure, then choose a feature that exists in the object and plot it over the image. The code uses Snap25 and Mbp as example labels only; their presence, biological relevance, and pattern depend on species, assay, tissue, and feature naming. Inspect the image key and color scale before interpreting a spatial gradient.

Python

sq.pl.spatial_scatter(adata, color=["total_counts", "Snap25"], img_alpha=0.5, cmap="magma")

R

SpatialFeaturePlot(spatial_data, features = c("nCount_Spatial", "Snap25")) &
  theme(legend.position = "right")

The returned R figure combines panels with patchwork. Its & operator applies the legend theme to every panel; using + here only styles the last panel and can leave the QC colorbar cramped above the first plot.

Calculate total_counts before normalization and log transformation, as above. It then records raw counts per spot; recomputing it from log-transformed expression would no longer measure library size. The marker panel uses the processed expression matrix, so its values are on a different scale from the raw-count QC panel.

Squidpy's spatial_scatter is the current image-overlay plotting API. Older Scanpy examples use sc.pl.spatial, but current Scanpy documentation marks it deprecated in favor of Squidpy's plot. A quick success check is: nonzero observations and features; nonempty, finite library-size values; a tissue image visible beneath spatially aligned spots; and a readable color scale for QC and the selected marker. Library size is a QC view, not a universal pass/fail threshold. If the image is absent or spots are displaced, verify the input's spatial/ files, library key, and image/coordinate scale; if the marker is missing, choose an observed feature and the intended assay/layer. Do not continue to biological interpretation until these checks pass.

3. Cluster expression profiles, then inspect their locations

Expression-neighbor clustering groups observations by transcriptional similarity. It does not by itself define spatial domains. Build the expression graph, cluster, and then display cluster labels in tissue coordinates. A spatial-neighbor graph is a separate choice for spatial statistics and should be constructed only when the question and coordinate system justify it.

Python

sc.pp.pca(adata)
sc.pp.neighbors(adata)
sc.tl.leiden(adata, key_added="clusters")
sq.pl.spatial_scatter(adata, color="clusters", img_alpha=0.4)

R

spatial_data <- RunPCA(spatial_data, assay = "SCT", verbose = FALSE)
spatial_data <- FindNeighbors(spatial_data, reduction = "pca", dims = 1:30)
spatial_data <- FindClusters(spatial_data, verbose = FALSE)
SpatialDimPlot(spatial_data, label = TRUE, label.size = 3)

These are compact workflow fragments, not a fully specified analysis: package versions, feature filtering, dimensionality choices, clustering resolution, and reproducibility settings need to be chosen and recorded for the dataset. A cluster boundary can reflect cell mixture, tissue composition, depth, or technical structure. Compare the map with morphology and QC before assigning a tissue-domain label.

mkdir -p data results printf "value 8.9 9.8 10.4 9.5 " > data/control.csv printf "value 11.2 10.7 12.1 11.4 " > data/treated.csv

For Python, use Python 3 and install NumPy, pandas, and SciPy 1.11 or newer in an environment you manage; save the displayed code as compare_groups.py. No R packages are needed for the base R route. start-here.html.before:
Software setup and practical references

Micromamba environments isolate a project's software. You need terminal comfort and permission to install packages. The collection is not standardized on one Python or R version; follow each lesson's dependencies.

Continue to command-line Part 2 or Part 3 when needed. In Part 1, zero-byte placeholder files are not sequencing data.

Look up data formats, statistics for independent two-group comparisons, or study design and batch effects as needed. Workflow automation and containers are optional.
